textbookText: Separation of Mixtures Introduction The mixing of two or more than two substances results in the impure substance. Impure substances are also known as mixtures. Mixtures are of homogeneous or heterogeneous types. There are various techniques employed to separate the components of a mixture. The technique depends on the nature of the components.
EXPERIMENT NO. 1
Object: TO OBTAIN SAND IN PURE AND DRY STATE FROM THE
MIXTURE OF SAND AND COMMON SALT
APPARATUS REQUIRED
Glass rod
2. Beaker
1. Funnel
Filter paper
5. Test tubes
4. Stand
CHEMICALS REQUIRED
1. Silver nitrate solution
2. Mixture of sand and common salt
THEORY

The soluble and insoluble components of a mixture can be separated by dissolving the mixture in water followed by filtration. Sand and common salt are separated from their mixture by dissolving the mixture in water followed by filtration.
Filtration can be defined as the method of separating the insoluble COmponent and solution of the soluble component by means of a porous

Practical Chemistry medium like filter paper, glass wool etc. The insoluble component, here sand, is obtained on the filter paper as residue. The solution of the soluble component, here common salt, which passes through the filter paper- is collected in the beaker. Thus received solution is called filtrate.
The purity of sand can be checked by treating sand-washed water with few drops of silver nitrate solution. Presence of common salt in sand is indicated by formation of a curdy white precipitate.

PROCESS
Figure 2.1: Folding a filter paper rod Liquid Filter paper Filtrate Figure 2.2: Filtration
Separation of Mixtures Take the given mixture of sand and common salt in a beaker. Add sufficient water little at a time stirring continuously with a glass rod to dissolve the common salt.
Warm the mixture solution gently. Allow the sand to settle down by standing the mixture for sometime.
Then, decant off the supernatant clear liquid. Add water, and repeat this process 3-4 times.
Now fold the filter paper as shown in figure and fit into the funnel.
Fit the apparatus as shown in figure. In this process, the stem of the funnel should touch the inner wall of the beaker whereby there will be no loss of liquid.
Transfer the supernatant liquid into the funnel by means of a glass rod. The filter paper should not be filled more than 2/ 3rd of it.
Add a little water in the beaker. Allow the mixture soluüon to stand for some time to settle and filter off the supernatant liquid. Repeat this process 2-3 times.

Take few drops of filtrate in a test tube directly from the stem of the funnel. Add few drops of silver nitrate solution. Formaåon of a curdy white precipitate indicates the presence of common salt in sand.
If a curdy white precipitate is seen, wash the sand again and check the sand-washed water with few drops of AgN03 solution. Repeat the process of washing till no any precipitate is seen.
Transfer all the sand on to the filter paper.
Remove the filter paper carefully from the funnel. Spread it over the wire gauze.
Dry the sand over the Bunsen burner or in air oven.

RESULT
Sand was obtained in pure and dry state from their mixture by dissolving the mixture in water followed by filtration, washing and drying.
PRECAUTIONS
While filtering, the solution should not come up to the rim of the filter paper.
The stem of the funnel should touch the inner wall of the beaker.
While drying the sand, care should be taken so that the filter paper does not burn.
Filtration should be done using a glass rod.
All the glasswares should be handled with care.
Note: Evaporate the filtrate to dryness to get the solid common salt.
